title: Bootstrapping the Express server
idea: `app.js` builds the Express app and exports it. `server.js` imports it, reads `PORT` and calls `listen`. In the project, only `server.js` opens a port.
points: `express.json()` runs first, so later handlers can read `req.body`.
`GET /health` returns a small JSON object, a quick check that the server answers.
`PORT` comes from the environment, a setting outside your code. 3000 is the fallback.
`app.listen` returns the HTTP server. Call `server.close()` to stop it.

hero.title: Two files, two jobs

left.title: src/app.js builds
items: Later lessons mount the routers here
Exports the app and never calls `listen`

hero.verdict: Importing `app.js` opens no port, so a test can start the app on port 0.

code.title: app.js and server.js
code.caption: Each `// src/...` block is its own file in the project. Add `export default app` to `app.js` and `import app from './app.js'` to `server.js`.

walk.text: Setup for this book: `PORT=0` makes the system pick a free port.
Create the app. Nothing listens yet.
Parse JSON bodies first, so every later handler can read `req.body`.
Reply with a small JSON object. It only proves that the process answers.
Read `PORT` as a number. An unset or empty `PORT` falls back to 3000.
`listen` opens the port and returns the HTTP server, which you can close later.
Setup: call the app once, print the reply, then close the server.

code.title: package.json
code.caption: The starting `package.json`. `npm install express` adds the dependency; `npm start` runs `node src/server.js`.

pitfalls: Never call `listen` in `app.js`: every import would try to open a port.
Do not hard-code the port. Read `PORT` so the environment can choose it.

quiz.why: An empty string is falsy, so `||` falls back to 3000. With `??` the empty string would stay, and `Number('')` is `0`.

takeaway: `app.js` builds the app; `server.js` only starts it.
